body.working_title: Bias of the occurrence probability in iETS inverse-odds and odds-ratio models

body.text: Are the occurrence probability and point forecasts of the iETS inverse-odds-ratio (iETS_I) and odds-ratio (iETS_O) models biased when estimated with the error proxies of Svetunkov and Boylan (2023), and how does any bias compare with that of Croston's method?

body.definition: Inverse odds ratio occurrence model (Svetunkov and Boylan 2023, eq. 18): o_t ~ Bernoulli(p_t), p_t = 1/(1+mu_b,t), mu_b,t = l_b,t-1, l_b,t = l_b,t-1 (1 + alpha_b e_b,t); in smooth: occurrence='inverse-odds-ratio' (C++ case 'i' in src/headers/ssOccurrence.h).
Odds ratio occurrence model (Svetunkov and Boylan 2023, eq. 16): p_t = mu_a,t/(mu_a,t+1), mu_a,t = l_a,t-1, l_a,t = l_a,t-1 (1 + alpha_a e_a,t); in smooth: occurrence='odds-ratio' (C++ case 'o').

Proxy for the unobservable occurrence error (Svetunkov and Boylan 2023, eqs. 24-25): u_t = (1 + o_t - p_hat_t)/2; iETS_O: 1 + e_a,t = u_t/(1-u_t); iETS_I: 1 + e_b,t = (1-u_t)/u_t. With an additive-error occurrence state (smooth's EA='A') the state is updated with log(1 + e) instead.
The recursion that produces p_hat_t from the observed o_t, the initial level and the smoothing parameter, with the state updated through the error proxy on every observation.
Croston (1972): SES on demand intervals q and sizes z, updated only at demand occurrences; probability forecast 1/q_hat.
Long-run mean of p_hat_t produced by an occurrence filter applied to o_t ~ Bernoulli(p) with constant p, after a burn-in; compared with the true p.
Simulated o_t, independent Bernoulli(p) draws with p fixed over time.

body.definition: The proxy for the unobservable occurrence error that smooth uses (occurrenceError() in src/headers/ssOccurrence.h): v_t = o_t - p_hat_t, u_t = (1 + v_t)/2; iETS_O: 1 + e_a,t = u_t/(1-u_t) = (1+v_t)/(1-v_t); iETS_I: 1 + e_b,t = (1-u_t)/u_t. With an additive occurrence error the log of the same ratio is used.
body.source: Svetunkov, I. and Boylan, J.E. (2023). iETS: State space model for intermittent demand forecasting. International Journal of Production Economics 265, 109013. doi:10.1016/j.ijpe.2023.109013 (eqs. 24-25, Appendix A)

body.definition: Croston (1972): SES on demand intervals q and sizes z, updated only at demand occurrences; probability forecast 1/q_hat.
body.source: Croston, J.D. (1972). Forecasting and stock control for intermittent demands. Operational Research Quarterly 23(3), 289-303.

body.definition: Proxy proposed in this study: the score of the Bernoulli occurrence log-likelihood o log p + (1-o) log(1-p) with respect to the log of the state, at p_hat_t: e_a,t = o_t - p_hat_t (mu_a: iETS_O, iETS_G) and e_b,t = p_hat_t - o_t (mu_b: iETS_I, iETS_G). Additive error: log mu_t = log mu_t-1 + alpha e_t (a score-driven filter with unit scaling); multiplicative error: mu_t = mu_t-1 (1 + alpha e_t). Derivation: derivations.md section 4.
body.source: Creal, D., Koopman, S.J. and Lucas, A. (2013). Generalized autoregressive score models with applications. Journal of Applied Econometrics 28(5), 777-795. doi:10.1002/jae.1279; Harvey, A.C. (2013). Dynamic Models for Volatility and Heavy Tails. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CBO9781139540933

body.definition: For an occurrence filter applied to o_t ~ Bernoulli(p), the value x of p_hat at which the expected update of the state, E[e_t | p_hat_t = x], is zero (derivations.md section 1).

Observation-driven time series models whose time-varying parameter is updated by a scaled score of the conditional log-likelihood (generalised autoregressive score / dynamic conditional score models).

body.definition: Recursions theta_t = theta_t-1 + alpha H(theta_t-1, o_t) with fixed gain alpha; as alpha tends to 0 their iterates concentrate around the stable zeros of the mean dynamics d theta/dt = E[H(theta, o)] (the ODE method).

body.statement: For every p in (0,1), the [[TM10:old error proxy]] has a non-zero expected value at the true probability: with o ~ Bernoulli(p) and p_hat = p, E[1 + e_a] = 2 - p + (1-p)^2/(1+p) > 1 and E[1 + e_b] = 1 + p + p^2/(2-p) > 1 (multiplicative error), and E[log(1 + e_a)] = -E[log(1 + e_b)] is positive for p < 0.5, zero at 0.5 and negative above (additive error); the cause is the convexity of the proxy in the unbiased residual o - p_hat.

body.text: Code check (no runs): smooth encodes additive-error occurrence models with an exponent. The ETS state x is on the log-odds scale (odds-ratio) or log inverse-odds scale (inverse-odds-ratio); the probability is exp(x)/(1+exp(x)) or 1/(1+exp(x)) (omLinkFunction in R/om.R; occurrenceLinkJac in src/headers/adamGradient.h); initial values are log-transformed (om_initial_transform in R/om.R); occurrenceError() returns log(u/(1-u)) or log((1-u)/u) and the state is updated additively. filter.cpp's additive branch is this recursion, so RN1-RN14 apply to smooth's additive models. Python compiles the same occurrenceError() through src/headers/adamCore.h (src/python/adamPython.cpp). Under this encoding dp/dx = +-p(1-p), so the additive score proxy o - p_hat (odds-ratio) or p_hat - o (inverse-odds-ratio) is the exact score of the log-likelihood with respect to smooth's own state.

body.definition: The update of a multiplicative level under ets="adam" in smooth: mu_t = mu_t-1 (1 + e_t)^alpha, i.e. log mu_t = log mu_t-1 + alpha log(1 + e_t) (adamGvalue() in src/headers/adamGeneral.h, case MNN); conventional ETS uses mu_t = mu_t-1 (1 + alpha e_t).
body.source: Svetunkov, I. (2023). Forecasting and Analytics with the Augmented Dynamic Adaptive Model (ADAM). Chapman and Hall/CRC. https://openforecast.org/adam/

body.definition: Proxy for multiplicative occurrence error under the ADAM ETS update: 1 + e_t = exp(s_t), with s_t the score proxy (o_t - p_hat_t for mu_a, p_hat_t - o_t for mu_b), so that log(1 + e_t) = s_t (derivations.md section 5).

The score proxy used with multiplicative occurrence error in the form 1 + e_t = 1 + s_t, s_t = o_t - p_hat_t (mu_a) or p_hat_t - o_t (mu_b); the form tested with conventional ETS in RN10 and RN12 (derivations.md section 4).

RN24 shows why: with ets="adam" the quantiles are simulated (two R runs with different seeds differ by up to 2.73, two Python runs by up to 1.83, with either proxy), while those of conventional ETS are analytical (equal across seeds and languages).

The iETS models of the M5 experiment run in Python (ADAM), faster than R by RN23 and equal to R where the computation is deterministic; Croston, SBA and TSB (tsintermittent) and HSP and NegBin (counter) have no Python implementation and run in R. The simulated quantiles of ets="adam" use a fixed seed per series and model, and 10,000 paths (the default).

body.text: Interpretation 1 of the M5 results (not tested): the score proxy helps where the ratio-proxy bias was large. With conventional ETS the ratio proxy biases iETS_O and iETS_I in opposite directions, as derived (derivations.md); on M5 the mean sCE moves from -6.74 to +1.77 for iETS_O and from +4.05 to -0.53 for iETS_I, and the mean RMSSE of iETS_O from 0.799 to 0.742. The true probability is unobservable on M5, so this shift is indirect evidence of the bias.

Interpretation 2 (not tested): iETS_G and iETS_A barely change because they were already close to unbiased. In iETS_G, p = mu_a/(mu_a + mu_b), and the ratio proxy pushes the two states in opposite directions, so their drifts largely cancel; iETS_A mostly selects among these models. iETS_G and iETS_A with the ratio proxy were the best iETS models on RMSSE (RN38), and their score-minus-ratio differences under conventional ETS were not significant (RN35).

Interpretation 3 (not tested): the result against the prediction in PL31 (iETS_I_ratio_conv at 0.99) is the bias being accidentally useful. The ratio proxy pushes iETS_I's probability up, which raises its upper quantiles; at 0.99 this helped (second only to HSP in the 0.99 MCB, RN38). Removing the bias lowers them, which also explains why the mean RMSSE of iETS_I_conv rises (0.742 to 0.750) while the median series improves. This suggests that the conventional-ETS iETS predictive distribution is too narrow in the far tail and that the bias masked it.

Interpretation 4 (not tested): the proxies differ as much in reactivity as in bias. When p_hat is small and a demand occurs, the ratio proxy gives 1 + e = u/(1-u) = (2 - p_hat)/p_hat, a jump of about 2/p_hat, close to Croston's interval update; the score proxy moves the log state by o - p_hat, at most 1. The ratio proxy is therefore far more reactive after long runs of zeros and the score proxy unbiased but sluggish; on non-stationary retail series the reactivity may be worth more than the unbiasedness, which would explain the small gains outside the badly biased iETS_O and iETS_I.

Interpretation 5 (not tested): two mechanisms likely shrink the effect of the bias on real data. (a) The bias is O(alpha) and the occurrence alpha is estimated by likelihood, so estimation can partly offset the drift (a small alpha, the initial level); the simulations used a fixed alpha, and the estimated M5 alphas have not been examined. (b) An upper quantile depends on p mostly through whether P(y = 0) exceeds tau, which switches the quantile between 0 and a positive value; small corrections of p rarely cross that point.

Interpretation 6 (not tested): the quantile gap between iETS and NegBin/HSP comes from the demand-size model, not the occurrence proxy. NegBin and HSP rank better at 0.80-0.95 with either proxy (RN38); iETS models sizes with a continuous Gamma ETS(M,N,N), they with count distributions. The ADAM ETS iETS models under-cover at every level (about 0.92 at 0.95), and rounding the quantiles up does not repair it (H23 and H24 not supported, RN40 and RN41), so the shortfall is not about discreteness.

body.definition: Proposed, not implemented: the score proxy scaled by the inverse Fisher information of the Bernoulli log-odds, s_t = (o_t - p_hat_t)/(p_hat_t (1 - p_hat_t)), used in place of o_t - p_hat_t for mu_a (and its negative for mu_b), with the same conventional and ADAM ETS forms as the score proxy (1 + alpha s, and exp(s) - 1 under ets='adam'). E[s_t] = 0 at p_hat_t = p for any positive scaling, so the zero-drift property of the score proxy holds; after a long run of zeros (p_hat small, o_t = 1) s_t is about 1/p_hat, close to the reactivity of the ratio proxy. Scaled scores of this kind are the inverse-information scaling of score-driven (GAS) models (Creal, Koopman and Lucas 2013).
